candidate.answerReason: The midsegment length and both areas remain fixed. The perimeter varies, so exactly one quantity changes.

methods.label: Track the fixed base and height
methods.explanation:
The useful observation is that moving \(P\) parallel to \(AB\) keeps its perpendicular distance from \(AB\) fixed. Write \(AB=b>0\) and let this fixed distance be \(h>0\).

Since \(M\) and \(N\) are side midpoints, the triangle midsegment theorem gives
\[
MN=\frac b2.
\]
Thus quantity (a) stays fixed. The area of \(\triangle PAB\) is \(bh/2\), so quantity (c) also stays fixed.

To find the trapezoid's area, subtract \(\triangle PMN\) from \(\triangle PAB\). Triangles \(PMB\) and \(PAB\) have bases \(PM\) and \(PA\) on the same line and share the altitude from \(B\). Since \(PM=PA/2\), the first triangle has half the area of the second. Similarly, triangles \(PMN\) and \(PMB\) share the altitude from \(M\) to line \(PB\), and \(PN=PB/2\). Consequently, \(\triangle PMN\) has one quarter of the area of \(\triangle PAB\). Therefore
\[
\operatorname{Area}(ABNM)
=\frac34\cdot\frac{bh}{2}
=\frac{3bh}{8},
\]
which is fixed, so quantity (d) does not change.

The perimeter \(PA+PB+b\) does vary. As \(P\) travels arbitrarily far along its line, its horizontal separation from \(A\) grows without bound, so \(PA\) also grows without bound. The perimeter therefore cannot remain constant.

Only quantity (b) changes. The answer is \(\boxed{1}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
